cards.title: Redundancy — No Single Point of Failure
cards.teaser: Redundancy means running multiple copies of every critical component so that the failure of any one copy does not bring the system down. It is the foundation of all reliability architecture.

runs.text: A
single point of failure (SPOF)

is any component whose failure causes the whole system to fail. Eliminating SPOFs is the first goal of reliability engineering. The method is redundancy: run enough copies of each component that losing any individual instance is a non-event.
Redundancy exists at every layer of a production system:

items.text: multiple application instances behind a load balancer. One instance dying sheds traffic to the others without user impact.
database primaries with read replicas; RAID across disks; object storage with cross-region replication. A single disk failure must not be a data-loss event.
multiple uplinks, multiple ISPs, anycast routing. A single provider outage must not partition you from the internet.
dual power supplies on servers, redundant PDUs, generator + UPS in data centers. The electrical layer is often the most neglected.
multiple nameservers in different autonomous systems. A single authoritative DNS server is a SPOF the size of your entire domain.

runs.text: Redundancy is not free — it costs money, increases operational complexity, and requires testing to verify it actually works (a replica that has never been promoted is not redundancy; it is a backup that may or may not restore). But the cost of a SPOF failure at production scale is always higher.

Untested redundancy is a false comfort. Run failure drills (chaos engineering) to verify that your redundant components actually take over under realistic failure conditions. A failover that has never been exercised often fails to fire when needed.
Redundancy means having enough copies that any one copy can fail and nobody notices. Every component that exists only once is a threat to your uptime.

cards.title: N+1 Redundancy — The Standard Target
cards.teaser: N+1 means running one more instance than you need to serve peak load. If N instances handle your traffic, you run N+1 — so that losing one still leaves you at exactly capacity. It is the canonical redundancy target for production services.

runs.text: The notation comes from capacity planning. If your service requires
N
instances to serve traffic at peak, an N+1 deployment runs one extra. That extra instance is not waste — it is your failure margin.
N+1 provides exactly one failure tolerance:

items.text: N+1 instances share load. Each runs at roughly N/(N+1) capacity — slightly underloaded, which is intentional.
N instances remain, running at 100% capacity. Traffic is served; the system is degraded but functional. Alerts fire; ops team replaces the failed instance.
N-1 instances remain; you are now overloaded. This is the boundary of N+1 protection.

runs.text: For higher availability requirements, N+2 or 2N (active-active across two sites) are used. Cloud providers typically target N+2 within an availability zone and 2N across zones.

N+1 also applies to non-compute resources: if you need one load balancer, deploy two. If you need one database primary, have one warm replica that can promote. The pattern is universal; only the instantiation cost varies.

Kubernetes Deployments default to a rolling update strategy that maintains availability during deploys — but only if you have enough replicas. A Deployment with replicas: 1 has no rollout redundancy. Set replicas to at least 2 and configure maxUnavailable: 0 to guarantee N+1 behavior during updates.
N+1 means "one more than you need": if you need 3 servers to handle traffic, run 4. That way, one can die and you still have enough.

cards.title: Bulkheads — Isolating Failures
cards.teaser: A bulkhead partitions a system so that a failure in one partition cannot flood the others. Borrowed from naval architecture, bulkheads in software take the form of separate thread pools, connection pools, and process boundaries.

runs.text: In a ship's hull, bulkheads are watertight compartments. If one compartment floods, the others remain dry and the ship stays afloat. In distributed systems, the same principle prevents a slow or failing dependency from exhausting shared resources and bringing down unrelated functionality.
The most common bulkhead patterns:

explanation.text:
WITHOUT bulkheads:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Service A                          │
│  Thread pool (50 threads total)     │
│                                     │
│  → Payments API   ─────────────┐    │
│  → Catalog API    ─────────────┤ SHARED POOL
│  → Rec Engine     ─────────────┘    │
│                                     │
│  If Rec Engine is slow:             │
│    all 50 threads pile up there     │
│    Payments + Catalog starve        │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

WITH bulkheads:
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Service A                          │
│                                     │
│  [Payments pool: 15 threads]        │
│  [Catalog pool:  20 threads]        │
│  [Rec Engine pool: 15 threads]      │
│                                     │
│  If Rec Engine is slow:             │
│    only its 15 threads are blocked  │
│    Payments + Catalog unaffected    │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

items.text: each downstream dependency gets its own thread pool. A slow dependency blocks only its own pool, not the shared executor. Netflix Hystrix pioneered this pattern for JVM services.
each downstream service gets its own database or HTTP connection pool. A connection leak to one service cannot exhaust connections for others.
running high-risk workloads (batch jobs, ML inference) in separate processes or containers prevents resource starvation in the primary service.

runs.text: Bulkheads pair naturally with circuit breakers (covered next). Together they form the core of the Hystrix resilience model: the circuit breaker stops calling a broken dependency; the bulkhead ensures those stopped calls cannot drain thread resources while the circuit opens.
A bulkhead divides your resources — threads, connections — into separate pools per downstream. When one downstream breaks, it only floods its own compartment. The rest of the ship stays dry.

cards.title: Circuit Breakers — Fail Fast
cards.teaser: A circuit breaker wraps downstream calls and stops making them when the downstream is clearly unhealthy. Instead of letting every request hang and time out, it fails fast, preserving resources and giving the downstream time to recover.

runs.text: The electrical analogy is exact: a circuit breaker trips when current exceeds safe levels, cutting power to prevent damage. In software, it trips when error rates or latency exceed a threshold, cutting calls to prevent resource exhaustion.
A circuit breaker has three states:

explanation.text:
failure threshold exceeded
  CLOSED ──────────────────────────────────────► OPEN
  (calls pass through)                           (calls fail immediately)
       ▲                                              │
       │                                    recovery timeout expires
       │                                              │
       │           probe call succeeds               ▼
       └──────────────────────────────── HALF-OPEN
                                          (one probe call allowed)

items.text: — normal operation. All calls pass through to the downstream. The breaker counts failures. While the error rate stays below threshold (e.g., <50% over a 10-second window), the circuit stays closed.

— downstream is unhealthy. All calls fail immediately without touching the downstream. The caller receives a fallback response (cached data, empty result, error). This protects the downstream from a flood of requests during recovery and preserves caller threads.
— the recovery timeout has elapsed. The breaker allows one probe call through. If it succeeds, the circuit closes. If it fails, the circuit reopens and the recovery timeout resets.

runs.text: Netflix Hystrix (open-sourced in 2012, placed in maintenance in 2018) made circuit breakers mainstream in microservice architectures. Its successor for the JVM ecosystem is Resilience4j. At the infrastructure level, Envoy Proxy implements circuit breaking and outlier detection natively in the sidecar, removing the need for per-service library integration.

Envoy's outlier detection ejects hosts from the load balancer pool when their error rate or latency exceeds thresholds. This is circuit breaking at the network layer: no application code required. Configure it with outlier_detection in the cluster config.

A circuit breaker watches calls to a downstream. If too many fail, it trips open and stops trying — failing immediately instead of waiting. After a timeout, it tries one call; if that works, it resets. Three states: closed (normal), open (failing fast), half-open (testing recovery).

cards.title: Circuit Breaker — Implementation Sketch
cards.teaser: Understanding circuit breaker states conceptually is necessary but not sufficient. Seeing the state machine in code reveals the design decisions: window sizing, threshold tuning, and what fallback behavior looks like.

runs.text: A minimal circuit breaker in Python illustrates the state machine. Production implementations (Resilience4j, Polly, go-circuit-breaker) add sliding windows, half-open concurrency limits, and metrics — but the skeleton is the same:
Key design decisions visible in the code:

items.text: the caller provides a fallback value to return when the circuit is open. This is where graceful degradation connects to circuit breaking — you need a sensible degraded response ready.
too low and you trip on transient blips; too high and you let a broken downstream drain resources. Start at 50% error rate over a 10-second window in production.
production implementations use a semaphore so that only one thread makes the probe call in HALF_OPEN state, rather than letting concurrent threads pile up.

runs.text: The circuit breaker code is just a state machine: count failures until threshold, then stop calling and start a timer. When the timer expires, try once. If it works, reset. If it fails, wait again.

cards.title: Load Shedding — Dropping Work to Survive
cards.teaser: Load shedding is the deliberate act of refusing work when the system is overloaded. It is a controlled failure: you choose what to drop so the system can continue serving the most important requests, rather than letting everything fail together.

runs.text: Without load shedding, an overloaded service enters a failure spiral: the queue grows, latency climbs, threads exhaust, and eventually nothing succeeds. The load that caused the overload is still being accepted, making recovery impossible without external intervention.
Load shedding breaks the spiral by saying:
when my capacity is exceeded, I will reject requests immediately
. Rejected requests receive an HTTP 503 (Service Unavailable) or 429 (Too Many Requests) immediately — they do not enter the queue and do not consume threads.
Shedding strategies differ in what they drop:

items.text: if the incoming queue exceeds a depth threshold, reject new arrivals. Simple to implement; preserves in-flight work.
assign work a priority (critical, normal, background). Under load, drop background work first, then normal, preserving critical paths. Google's Borg scheduler uses this for cluster workloads.

measure CPU utilization or p99 latency continuously. When a signal crosses a threshold, activate shedding automatically. The Linux kernel's Completely Fair Scheduler applies adaptive mechanisms to CPU time-slicing.

runs.text: Load shedding is distinct from rate limiting (which limits per-caller inbound rate) and throttling (which caps per-tenant sustained throughput). Shedding is a system-internal self-protection mechanism activated by the service's own resource exhaustion — not by who is calling.

A 503 returned in 1ms is not a failure — it is information. The caller can retry, backoff, or route to a fallback. A request that hangs for 30 seconds and then times out consumes your threads for the full duration and leaves the caller worse off. Fast rejection beats slow failure.
Load shedding means deliberately saying "no" to some requests when you are overloaded, so you can keep saying "yes" to the important ones. A fast rejection is better than a slow collapse.

cards.title: Graceful Degradation — Partial Beats Zero
cards.teaser: Graceful degradation means delivering reduced but meaningful functionality when a dependency fails, rather than failing the entire response. The goal is to keep the user-facing surface functional even when internal components are broken.

runs.text: Full functionality requires every dependency to be healthy. Graceful degradation accepts that some dependencies will be unavailable and plans what the product experience looks like in those states.
Classic examples from real systems:

items.text: if the recommendations engine is down, show static popular-items instead. The page loads; the cart works; checkout is unaffected. Only the personalized section degrades.
if real-time engagement counts cannot be fetched, display cached counts from 5 minutes ago. Users see slightly stale numbers rather than an error page.
if the permissions service is down but authentication succeeds, grant read-only access from a cached permissions snapshot rather than refusing login entirely.
if ML-ranked search is unavailable, fall back to keyword-only search. Less relevant but functional.

runs.text: Graceful degradation requires deliberate design at the product layer, not just the infrastructure layer. Engineering must define — in advance — what each dependency's fallback behavior is. "Return 500 if the recommendations service is down" is not graceful degradation; it is a missed opportunity.
The implementation typically uses circuit breakers with fallback values, cached responses via CDN or Redis, and feature flags that can disable non-critical features when their backing services fail.

Amazon's well-known example: the shopping cart is owned by a separate service with an independent data store. Even if most of Amazon.com is degraded, the cart and checkout path remain functional. Critical paths are designed to have zero non-critical dependencies in their hot path.
Graceful degradation means planning, in advance, what a reduced but still useful experience looks like when parts of the system are broken. Partial functionality beats a blank error page.

cards.title: Timeouts — Every External Call Has One
cards.teaser: A timeout is the maximum time you are willing to wait for a response. Without one, a single slow downstream can hold threads open indefinitely. Timeout discipline is one of the most impactful and most neglected reliability practices.

runs.text: An external call without a timeout is a thread leak waiting to happen. If the downstream hangs, the calling thread blocks indefinitely. With enough concurrent requests, all threads block, the thread pool exhausts, and the service stops responding to new requests — not because the service itself is broken, but because a dependency is slow.
Timeout discipline:

items.text: Set timeouts on every external call:
HTTP clients, database queries, cache lookups, queue operations. The default for most libraries is no timeout or a very large one (minutes). Set an explicit value.
Set connect and read timeouts separately:
a connect timeout (e.g., 1s) catches unreachable hosts; a read timeout (e.g., 5s) catches hosts that accept the connection but never respond. Both are needed.

if an upstream gave you 200ms to respond, your downstream call budget is less than 200ms. Propagate deadlines via gRPC deadline propagation or HTTP headers. Do not issue a 5-second downstream call on behalf of a 200ms upstream budget.

in a microservice chain A→B→C→D, each hop must leave room for the next. A common failure mode: A gives B 1s; B gives C 900ms; C gives D 800ms; D's p99 is 850ms — and the entire chain fails at C because nobody budgeted correctly.

explanation.text:
import httpx

# Always specify connect_timeout and read_timeout separately
with httpx.Client(
    timeout=httpx.Timeout(
        connect=1.0,   # give up connecting after 1s
        read=5.0,      # give up waiting for response after 5s
        write=2.0,
        pool=0.5,
    )
) as client:
    response = client.get("https://api.example.com/resource")

runs.text: The canonical timeout anti-pattern: setting a very large timeout (60s, 120s) because "we don't want it to fail." A 120-second timeout means a slow downstream can hold your thread for 2 minutes. At 100 concurrent requests, you can exhaust your thread pool in 2 minutes from a single slow endpoint.

A timeout is how long you are willing to wait before giving up. Without one, a single slow downstream can hold open every thread in your service. Set one on every external call, keep it tight, and propagate deadlines through the call chain.

cards.title: Retries with Exponential Backoff and Jitter
cards.teaser: Retrying failed calls is correct. Retrying immediately, at fixed intervals, and all at once is destructive. The AWS Architecture Blog pattern — exponential backoff with jitter — is the standard for safe retry behavior.

runs.text: When a downstream fails transiently, retrying is the right response. But naive retries — immediately, or at a fixed cadence — amplify the problem. If 1000 clients all fail at the same moment and immediately retry in lockstep, they generate a second wave of traffic identical in shape to the first, prolonging the overload. This is called a
retry storm
or thundering herd.
The AWS Architecture Blog (2015) formalized the canonical solution:
exponential backoff with full jitter
. The math:

explanation.text:
import random
import time

def retry_with_jitter(fn, max_retries=5,
                     base_delay=0.5, max_delay=30):
    """
    Exponential backoff with full jitter.
    Attempt k waits a random value in [0, min(cap, base * 2^k)].

    This spreads retries across time, preventing thundering herd.
    """
    for attempt in range(max_retries + 1):
        try:
            return fn()
        except TransientError as exc:
            if attempt == max_retries:
                raise  # exhausted retries

            # Exponential cap: base * 2^attempt, clamped to max_delay
            cap = min(max_delay, base_delay * (2 ** attempt))

            # Full jitter: pick uniformly from [0, cap]
            sleep_for = random.uniform(0, cap)

            time.sleep(sleep_for)

# Example wait times (base=0.5s, cap=30s):
# attempt 0: [0, 0.5]  → avg 0.25s
# attempt 1: [0, 1.0]  → avg 0.5s
# attempt 2: [0, 2.0]  → avg 1.0s
# attempt 3: [0, 4.0]  → avg 2.0s
# attempt 4: [0, 8.0]  → avg 4.0s

runs.text: The AWS blog evaluated four jitter strategies (no jitter, full jitter, equal jitter, decorrelated jitter) and found
full jitter
— uniformly random in [0, cap] — provided the best tradeoff between call success rate and load on the downstream. Decorrelated jitter performed similarly but is harder to reason about.

Only retry idempotent operations (reads, or writes protected by idempotency keys). Retrying a non-idempotent write — charging a credit card, sending an email — without idempotency protection is a reliability bug, not a fix.

Retrying immediately and all at once makes a failing system worse. Exponential backoff waits longer with each retry; jitter randomizes the wait so all clients do not pile up at the same moment. Together they give the downstream time to recover without being re-overwhelmed.

cards.title: Idempotency — Making Retries Safe
cards.teaser: An idempotent operation produces the same result regardless of how many times it is executed. Without idempotency, retries cause duplicate writes — double charges, duplicate records, duplicate emails. Idempotency keys are the standard mechanism.

runs.text: HTTP GET and DELETE are naturally idempotent: fetching or deleting the same resource twice has the same result as doing it once. HTTP POST is not: creating an order twice creates two orders. Idempotency keys make POST-like operations safe to retry.
The standard mechanism:

items.text: The client generates a unique idempotency key (UUID v4) for each logical operation.
The key is sent with the request (HTTP header:
The server stores the key and its result atomically after the first successful execution.
On subsequent requests with the same key, the server returns the stored result without re-executing.
Keys are retained for a window (e.g., 24 hours) then expired.

explanation.text:
# Client: generate key per logical operation, not per HTTP call
import uuid

idempotency_key = str(uuid.uuid4())  # generated once

for attempt in range(max_retries):
    response = requests.post(
        "/payments",
        json={"amount": 100, "currency": "USD"},
        headers={"Idempotency-Key": idempotency_key},  # same key every retry
    )
    if response.ok:
        break

# Server: check key before processing
def create_payment(request):
    key = request.headers["Idempotency-Key"]
    if cached := idempotency_store.get(key):
        return cached  # replay stored result

    result = process_payment(request.body)
    idempotency_store.set(key, result, ttl=86400)
    return result

runs.text: Idempotency keys are not only a client responsibility — they require server-side storage (Redis or a database table). The atomicity of "store key + execute operation" is critical: a race condition between two retries arriving simultaneously must result in only one execution.

An idempotency key is a unique ID the client sends with every retry of the same operation. The server uses it to recognize "I have already done this" and return the stored result instead of running it again. This is what makes retrying a payment safe.

cards.title: Rate Limiting — Capacity Protection at the Front Door
cards.teaser: Rate limiting caps the number of requests a caller can make over a time window. It protects the service from abusive or misbehaving callers and prevents any single client from consuming disproportionate capacity.

runs.text: Rate limiting operates at the front door of a service — typically in the API gateway or reverse proxy — before requests reach application logic. Its purpose is to protect the service, not to bill or meter users (that is throttling).
Common rate limiting algorithms:

items.text: each caller has a bucket that fills at a fixed rate (e.g., 100 tokens/second). Each request consumes one token. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected. Allows short bursts (bucket draining) without violating sustained rate.
requests enter a queue and drain at a fixed rate. Smooths traffic but does not allow bursts. Useful when downstream cannot handle spike traffic even briefly.
count requests per caller per N-second window. Simple to implement but vulnerable to double-rate attacks at window boundaries.
track exact timestamps of recent requests. Precise but memory-intensive. Used in GitHub's API rate limiter.

runs.text: Rate limiting responses: HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) with a
Retry-After
header indicating when the caller can retry. Well-behaved clients respect this header and back off accordingly. The header is part of RFC 6585 and is supported by most HTTP client libraries.
Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, Kong, and AWS API Gateway all implement rate limiting natively. In Nginx:

Rate limiting sets a cap on how many requests any one caller can make per second or per minute. It stops a single client from overwhelming the service. When the limit is hit, you return 429 and tell them when to try again.

cards.title: Throttling — Per-Tenant Capacity Caps
cards.teaser: Throttling is rate limiting applied at the tenant or customer level, enforcing fairness across multi-tenant systems. Where rate limiting protects the service from overload, throttling protects tenants from each other.

runs.text: In a SaaS platform, tenants share infrastructure. Without throttling, one large tenant's bursty traffic degrades performance for all others — the noisy neighbor problem. Throttling solves this by giving each tenant its own capacity envelope.
Throttling vs. rate limiting:

items.text: — system-level protection. Applies to anonymous or per-IP callers. Focuses on preventing overload.

— tenant-level fairness. Applies to authenticated callers with known identities. Focuses on equitable resource allocation. Often tied to pricing tiers (free: 100 req/min; pro: 1000 req/min; enterprise: custom).

runs.text: AWS implements throttling for every API service: EC2, S3, DynamoDB, Lambda all have per-account and per-service throttle limits. DynamoDB's provisioned throughput model is a per-table throttle: requests exceeding the configured RCU/WCU return
ProvisionedThroughputExceededException
, which clients must handle with backoff and retry.

Implementation typically uses a distributed counter (Redis) keyed by tenant ID and time window. The token bucket algorithm scales well for throttling because it allows tenants to burst up to their bucket size while enforcing sustained rate limits.

Communicate throttle limits to tenants clearly: publish them in API documentation, return current usage in response headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset), and provide a 429 with Retry-After. Tenants who understand their limits design better clients.
Throttling gives each customer their own speed limit. One customer hammering your API does not slow down everyone else. It is rate limiting with an identity attached.

cards.title: Dependency Analysis — Knowing What Brings You Down
cards.teaser: Every service has a set of dependencies whose failure cascades into its own failure. Mapping those dependencies, understanding their failure modes, and categorizing them by criticality is the foundation of reliability design.

runs.text: A service cannot be designed for reliability without knowing its failure surface. Dependency analysis — also called Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) in formal engineering disciplines — maps every dependency and characterizes what happens when it fails.
The dependency taxonomy:

items.text: if this dependency fails, the service cannot serve its core function at all. The auth service is a hard dependency for every authenticated API. These require circuit breakers, N+1 deployment, and clear SLAs.
if this dependency fails, core functionality continues but some features degrade. The recommendations engine is soft for e-commerce. These are candidates for graceful degradation.
called inline during request handling. Their latency directly adds to response time. Their failure blocks the response. Require timeouts and circuit breakers.
called via queue or event stream. Their failure is buffered. The producer continues; the consumer can catch up when it recovers. Require dead-letter queues (DLQs) and consumer lag monitoring.

runs.text: The output of dependency analysis is a dependency map for each service, with each dependency labeled:

Google's SRE book describes "dependency analysis" as a prerequisite to capacity planning and SLO design. You cannot set a meaningful availability target for your service without knowing the availability of its hard dependencies. If your service depends on three hard dependencies each at 99.9% availability, your theoretical maximum is 99.9%^3 = 99.7%.

Dependency analysis answers "what can take us down?" by mapping every upstream and downstream dependency, marking which are critical and which are optional, and specifying what happens when each one fails. You cannot design against failures you have not catalogued.
